prompt: What are the two honest outcomes of an improvement plan that the person has to be told?

choices.text: Closing the gap, or leaving
choices.why: Right: hiding either outcome is a form of dishonesty.

choices.text: Promotion or no promotion
choices.why: A plan is about a gap in the current role, not promotion.

choices.text: A pay rise if it goes well, and a pay cut if it does not, adjusted at the end of the period
choices.why: Pay is not one of the outcomes the lesson names.

choices.text: A transfer to another team, or staying
choices.why: Not the outcomes the lesson names.

prompt: A manager has already decided somebody must leave. What does the lesson say is the honest course?

choices.text: Say so, and use the real process
choices.why: Right: a plan nobody expects to be passed harms everybody, including the next person put on one.

choices.text: Write a plan anyway, as a record that a chance was given
choices.why: That is the dishonest version the lesson describes.

choices.text: Wait for the person to resign
choices.why: Waiting is not honest either, and it can take months.

choices.text: Make the plan’s expectations impossible to meet, so the outcome is certain and nobody wastes time
choices.why: That is the dishonest version with the cruelty made explicit.

prompt: Why did Renata believe Marcos could close the gap in six weeks?

choices.text: Plans always work if the support is good
choices.why: Marcos’s did not fully work, despite the support.

choices.text: Because Sônia told her it would be fine
choices.why: Sônia checked the plan; the belief was Renata’s own judgement.

choices.text: The gap was a habit, and he had already changed one habit in a month
choices.why: Right: and if she had not believed it, she would not have written a plan.

choices.text: Because his father was out of hospital by then and the other problems outside work had passed
choices.why: That mattered, but the reason given is that the gap was a habit he had shown he could change.

prompt: Match each part of a plan with the failure that ruins it.
hint: Five parts, five failures; four here.

prompt: Why does Marcos’s plan ask for four of six tickets, not six of six?

choices.text: Four is the company standard
choices.why: No standard is mentioned.

choices.text: To make it easier
choices.why: It is set to be fair, not easy.

choices.text: Estimates go wrong for everybody now and then, and a plan that demands perfection is designed to fail
choices.why: Right: the expectation has to be achievable as well as measurable.

choices.text: Because the other two tickets would be paired with Yara
choices.why: Pairing covers the first three, and they count like the others.

prompt: Why six weeks, by the lesson?
hint: Luck on one side, suspense on the other.

choices.text: Long enough to see a habit change, and short enough not to leave the team and Marcos in suspense for months
choices.why: Right: two weeks would measure luck; six months would be too long for the team and for Marcos.

choices.text: The law requires six weeks
choices.why: No such legal requirement is given.

choices.text: It matched the length of the sprint
choices.why: Sprints are not mentioned.

choices.text: Because that is how long Yara had available for pairing before her own deadline came up
choices.why: Yara paired on three tickets; the period was chosen for the habit.

prompt: Which sentence belongs in the expectation part of a plan, by the lesson’s standard?
hint: Could somebody else tell, at the end?

choices.text: “Be more reliable with estimates.”
choices.why: Vague: nobody could say at the end whether it was met.

choices.text: “When a ticket will exceed its estimate by more than half, say so within one working day.”
choices.why: Right: measurable, specific, and somebody else could check it.

choices.text: “Show more ownership.”
choices.why: A judgement dressed as a goal.

choices.text: “Stop being careless.”
choices.why: An adjective about the person, which belongs nowhere in a plan.

prompt: In week four, a ticket went to twice its estimate without a word. What did Renata’s weekly summary say?

choices.text: Good progress overall, to keep him motivated through the second half of the plan
choices.why: That is the failure the lesson warns about.

choices.text: Exactly that
choices.why: Right: a summary that says “good progress” in a bad week removes the evidence and misleads the person.

choices.text: Nothing; only good weeks are summarised
choices.why: Every week is summarised, good and bad.

choices.text: That the plan was over
choices.why: It ran its six weeks.

prompt: If Yara had not paired on the first three estimates, what would the lesson say about the plan?
hint: A plan binds the manager too.

choices.text: It still stands, since the expectation was clear
choices.why: The support was part of the agreement.

choices.text: It failed on Caju’s side, and could not fairly be held against Marcos
choices.why: Right: support promised and not given voids the plan.

choices.text: Marcos should have asked somebody else to pair with him instead
choices.why: The support was Caju’s to provide.

choices.text: It should be ended early, since the support had already broken down and could not be recovered
choices.why: The honest response is to say so and extend or restart, not to end it.

prompt: Put the three lines of each weekly summary in the order the lesson gives them.
hint: What happened, what was given, what next.
items: What was agreed for next week

prompt: When does the lesson consider extending a partly met plan honest?

choices.text: Whenever the manager is unsure
choices.why: Extending to avoid the decision is the dishonest version again.

choices.text: Never
choices.why: The lesson allows one extension with a reason.

choices.text: As many times as needed, as long as the person agrees each time
choices.why: Repeated extensions leave everybody in suspense and avoid the decision.

choices.text: Once, with a specific reason to think more time would close the gap
choices.why: Right: for example support that arrived late; not to avoid the decision.

prompt: Marcos’s plan required at least four of six tickets within one and a half times their estimate. He managed three. By how many tickets did he fall short?
Support promised and not given ___ the plan.
At the end of a plan, a manager says: “It went fine, let’s just keep an eye on things for a while,” without closing it formally. What does the lesson say is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; caution is sensible after a plan
choices.why: Caution that leaves the plan hanging is the failure named.

choices.text: He should have extended it formally
choices.why: If it was met, there is nothing to extend.

choices.text: The person is left wondering whether they are still on it
choices.why: Right: a met plan should be closed clearly, in a conversation and in writing.

choices.text: He should have started a new plan on a different area to keep the momentum going
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests a new plan after a met one.
